# The AWS map: global infrastructure, shared responsibility, Well-Architected: say it

<!-- speak:start id=aws-map-s02 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** Do we need a second Region to be highly available, or are Availability Zones enough?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** For most workloads, several Availability Zones in one Region are enough. Add a second Region for extreme resilience; an asynchronous copy there runs behind.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both protect you from failures. The difference is the size of the failure.

It works like this. An Availability Zone is one or more separate data centers inside a Region.

A fire or a flood in one zone does not reach the others.

So run production in at least two Availability Zones, and a zone failure won't stop you.

The zones are close, so your data can be copied synchronously between them.

A second Region protects you from the loss of a whole Region.

The thing to watch is that an asynchronous copy runs behind.

So a failover to the second Region can lose the last few writes.

And every component has to be duplicated in each Region.

In your case, I'd start with several zones in one Region, like most customers do.

What does your biggest customer's contract say about a Region outage?

**Skeleton.** both cover failures, different sizes / production in two zones / second Region for Region loss / asynchronous copies run behind

**Must say.**

- Most customers can reach their resilience goals in a single Region with Regional services or Multi-AZ architectures.
- Deploy every production workload in at least two Availability Zones (AZs) in a Region.
- A second Region is for workloads that require extreme resilience, assuming that the data residency requirements allow it.
- When a datastore is replicated asynchronously across Regions, a failover between Regions can lose data or leave it inconsistent.

**Do not say.**

- "You need a second Region to be highly available.". Say: Most customers reach their resilience goals in one Region. A multi-Region design when a Multi-AZ design meets the business requirements is an anti-pattern.
- "Our copy in the second Region is asynchronous, but a failover will lose nothing.". Say: An asynchronous copy between Regions runs behind. A failover between Regions can lose data or leave it inconsistent.
- "Several instances in one Availability Zone are highly available.". Say: If all of your instances are in one Availability Zone and that zone fails, none of them is available.

**Follow-up questions.**

- How much data could we lose if we fail over to the second Region? An asynchronous copy between Regions runs behind, so the latest writes can be lost. You decide how much loss is acceptable and write it down as the RPO: the maximum acceptable time since the last recovery point.
- If we add a second Region later, what has to run there? A copy of every component: the network, the compute and the data services. A component in one Region that depends on the other Region raises the risk of failure. Your data residency rules also have to allow the second Region.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=aws-map-s01 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** AWS says that it is secure. So why is the public bucket our problem and not theirs?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** AWS secures the cloud itself: the buildings, the hardware and the network. You secure what you put in it, including who can read your bucket.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: AWS secures the cloud, and you secure what you put in it.

It works like this. AWS protects the buildings, the hardware and the network that run its services.

For Amazon S3, AWS also runs the operating system and the storage platform.

Your part is the data. You choose how to encrypt it and who can read it.

You set those permissions with IAM, the AWS permissions service.

You keep control of those choices, as in your own data center.

The thing to watch is that a managed service doesn't hand your data decisions to AWS.

In your case, the bucket is public so that the browser can play recordings.

That setting is yours, so the fix is on your side too.

Which other buckets hold customer recordings today?

**Skeleton.** of the cloud: AWS / in the cloud: you / S3 data and permissions: you / public bucket is our setting

**Must say.**

- AWS is responsible for protecting the infrastructure that runs all of the services offered in the AWS Cloud: hardware, software, networking and facilities.
- For Amazon S3, AWS operates the infrastructure, the operating system and the platform; the customer manages the data and uses IAM to apply permissions.
- The customer is responsible for security in the cloud and keeps control of the security it chooses for its content.

**Do not say.**

- "S3 is a managed service, so AWS controls who can read our files.". Say: For S3, AWS runs the operating system and the platform. The customer manages the data and uses IAM to apply the permissions.
- "AWS is responsible for all security in the cloud.". Say: Security is shared. AWS handles security of the cloud, and the customer handles security in the cloud.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Does AWS at least keep our instance patched? No. On Amazon EC2, you patch the guest operating system and your applications, and AWS patches the infrastructure. On services such as Amazon S3 and DynamoDB, AWS applies the patches without any action from you.
- Is our part the same for every AWS service we use? No. Your part changes with the services and Regions you choose and with the laws that apply to you. On Amazon EC2 you also own the operating system and the security groups. On Amazon S3 you own the data and its permissions.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->
